dialogue_history.sentences_no_utterance_types: The core issue isn’t the NHS itself, it’s underfunding, and with proper government investment, we can slash waiting times while still protecting universal access. A system with targeted funding often leaves out vulnerable groups who fall through the cracks, whereas universal coverage catches those who’d otherwise die waiting. Progressive taxation can ease the hit on working families by targeting the wealthiest, while still ensuring the NHS gets the cash it needs to cut waiting lists. Less bureaucracy sounds nice, but it risks prioritising profit over people, while the NHS keeps the focus on saving every life possible with equal care. I believe universal access through the NHS saves more lives because it ensures everyone, no matter their income, gets treatment without delay or discrimination.

Why do you reckon a fully-funded NHS ensures true fairness when official data shows the 7 million waiting list persists despite billions in past funding, proving the universal model can't prioritise need over cash without market incentives to slash delays?
A beefed-up NHS doesn't deliver outcomes for everyone; it just spreads the misery equally through endless queues, while profit-focused mixed systems save more lives with real speed and innovation.

Why claim private options let the wealthy jump queues in market systems when competition drives efficiencies that speed up public tracks for the vulnerable, unlike the NHS's equal misery for everyone?
